title: Algebraic Fractions with Algebraic Denominator

findings.finding: The opening topic has no review of multiplying algebraic terms or recognising shared algebraic factors, although its worked examples use both.
findings.breakdown: Students must recall how powers combine in products and recognise the variable factors available for cancellation while following the new fraction methods.
findings.checked: All teaching was supplied. No review precedes p3, and p4 states the cancellation method without rehearsing these prior symbolic skills. Finding the highest common factor in one step is unnecessary because the examples cancel factors successively.
findings.assumptions: Algebraic products and recognition of common factors are prior learning from the separately listed algebra and index-law booklets. Calculators do not supply these symbolic decisions.

repair.proposal: Insert four short opening items: (a) Simplify 3a × 2b. Answer: 6ab. (b) Simplify 4b² × 3b⁵. Answer: 12b⁷. (c) Which is a factor of both 10a⁵ and 5a²: a² or a⁵? Answer: a². (d) Which is a factor of both 8ab and 2a²: a or a²? Answer: a. Keep the review within one page.

findings.doneWhen: A short opening review rehearses algebraic multiplication and recognition of shared variable factors.

findings.finding: Nine later practice parts repeat complete earlier tasks with unchanged expressions and no explicit retrieval or comparison purpose.
findings.breakdown: The later copies reuse the same operation, values and givens, allowing recall or copying of an earlier result instead of a fresh application.
findings.checked: Compared every targeted pair. The reminders to simplify before multiplying do not explicitly establish a comparison with the earlier copies. No targeted task has additional parts or changed givens that distinguish it.
findings.assumptions: The supplied order is the teaching order, and no instructional purpose for these exact repetitions is stated elsewhere.

repair.proposal: Retain the earlier copies and replace the later ones as follows. p6-q4-a: 42x²/(6x), answer 7x. p14-q1-a: (8x/5) × (7y/8), answer 7xy/5. p14-q1-c: (10a/7) × (3b/(4c)), answer 15ab/(14c). p14-q3-b: (7x/5) ÷ 3, answer 7x/15. p14-q3-c: 3 ÷ (x/5), answer 15/x. p14-q2-c: (7a/10) ÷ (1/4), answer 14a/5. p14-q2-e: (4/7) ÷ (2y/3), answer 6/(7y). p14-q2-g: (6a/7) ÷ (2/5), answer 15a/7. p18-q1-e: (5x³/(12y⁶)) ÷ (10x⁵/(3y²)), answer 1/(8x²y⁴).

findings.doneWhen: Each later copy uses different numbers while preserving its operation structure and type of simplification.

findings.finding: Follow part f with equivalent fractions that reverse which missing component students must recover.
findings.breakdown: Recovering a denominator uses the same multiplier relationship in the opposite direction; simplifying the completed fraction reconnects equivalence and cancellation.
findings.checked: The proposed answers are correct, and both equivalent fractions and cancellation have been taught by the end of this topic.
findings.assumptions: Use the original expressions' denominator restrictions; x ≠ 0.

repair.proposal: Append optional parts to p5-q1: (g) Complete 7w/(6x) = □/(54x³). Answer: 63wx². (h) Complete 7w/(6x) = 35wx/□. Answer: 30x². (i) Simplify 63wx²/(54x³). Answer: 7w/(6x).

findings.doneWhen: The optional follow-up retains the original fraction and includes the reverse missing-denominator task.

findings.finding: Choosing the lowest common denominator for unequal powers of the same pronumeral is required but never demonstrated.
findings.breakdown: In 5/a + 2/a³, students must recognise that a³ already contains a as a factor. The preceding examples do not expose this decision: their variable powers are either confined to one denominator or identical in both.
findings.checked: Searched the complete earlier teaching. Equivalent-fraction examples supply the destination denominator, and the simplification examples teach cancellation. Neither teaches selecting a common denominator for unequal powers. Using a⁴ can produce a correct but unreduced result; it does not demonstrate the stated lowest-common-multiple method.
findings.assumptions: Numerical LCM and index operations are prior knowledge. Selecting algebraic common multiples with unequal powers is a new variant here.

repair.proposal: Immediately before p8-guided-e-node, add: “For denominators a and a³, use a³: it already contains a as a factor. Since a × a² = a³, multiply the numerator and denominator of the first fraction by a²; the second fraction stays unchanged.” Leave students to complete the sum.

findings.doneWhen: The teaching explicitly connects the higher denominator power with the multiplier needed for the lower power.

findings.finding: Use the sum and difference in parts c and d to recover the original fractions.
findings.breakdown: Combining those results exposes how one original term cancels while the other doubles.
findings.checked: Parts c and d give 7x/10 and 3x/10. Their sum is x and their difference is 2x/5; halving recovers x/2 and x/5. All required operations are available by this topic's end.
findings.assumptions: No additional prior method or domain restriction is needed.

repair.proposal: Append optional parts after p10-q5-o: (p) Add your answers to c and d. Answer: x. (q) Halve your answer to p. Answer: x/2. (r) Subtract your answer to d from your answer to c. Answer: 2x/5. (s) Halve your answer to r. Answer: x/5. (t) Explain why q and s recover the two original fractions in c. Expected explanation: adding the sum and difference cancels the x/5 terms and doubles x/2; subtracting cancels the x/2 terms and doubles x/5.

findings.doneWhen: The optional parts connect the numerical algebraic results to cancellation and doubling of the original terms.

findings.finding: The final topic combines fraction operations with cancellation of powers but has no opening review of the latter method.
findings.breakdown: Both examples require deciding whether surviving powers belong above or below the fraction bar. This prior method must be recalled while multiplication or reciprocal multiplication is also being applied.
findings.checked: p4 teaches cancellation of powers. The immediately preceding topic practises ordinary fraction operations, cancellation of first powers and products producing powers, but does not rehearse the higher-power cancellation used in p17. These examples also combine methods from earlier topics, so the combined-method review exception applies.
findings.assumptions: Symbolic cancellation is prior learning, and calculators do not perform the required decisions.

repair.proposal: Insert before p17-information-block: “Simplify: (a) x⁶/x²; (b) y²/y⁵; (c) a³b⁵/(a³b²).” Answers: x⁴; 1/y³; b³. Keep this short review within one page.

findings.doneWhen: The review rehearses surviving numerator powers, surviving denominator powers and complete cancellation before the combined examples.

findings.finding: Add a run varying only the numerator exponent to expose where a surviving power appears.
findings.breakdown: The run crosses from a denominator power through complete cancellation to a numerator power, a central distinction without an existing comparable run.
findings.checked: All proposed answers are correct. The original denominators require the variables to be nonzero, including the part whose simplified answer is constant. Only taught multiplication and cancellation are required.
findings.assumptions: x ≠ 0 throughout the run and y ≠ 0 in the following question.

repair.proposal: Append to p18-q1 under its existing “Simplify” instruction. Add only this instruction: “Predict where the remaining x factor will be before simplifying.” Parts: (g) (x²/3) × (6/x⁴), answer 2/x²; (h) (x³/3) × (6/x⁴), answer 2/x; (i) (x⁴/3) × (6/x⁴), answer 2; (j) (x⁵/3) × (6/x⁴), answer 2x. Follow with unpatterned part (k) (2y³/5) × (15/y⁷), answer 6/y⁴. In g–j only the first numerator exponent changes; coefficients, denominator exponent and operation remain fixed.

findings.doneWhen: The optional run includes the cancellation boundary and is followed by the unpatterned application.

findings.finding: The equivalent-fraction examples introduce their multipliers without showing how the target denominators determine them.
findings.breakdown: The algebraic example requires choosing 3b⁵ before multiplying both parts. Showing that multiplier already inserted does not model this decision.
findings.checked: The preceding definition explains applying the same multiplier, but not choosing it. No earlier teaching supplies the algebraic calculation; the division index law appears afterwards in p4-indices-definition.
findings.assumptions: Students are learning equivalent algebraic fractions. Calculator use does not affect the symbolic decision.

repair.proposal: Add before the respective working: “Required multiplier: 14 ÷ 7 = 2.” and “Required multiplier: 12b⁷ ÷ 4b² = 3b⁵.”

findings.doneWhen: The examples explicitly derive their multipliers from the original and required denominators.

findings.finding: The introductory addition and subtraction examples supply algebraic common denominators without modelling their selection.
findings.breakdown: Students see equivalent numerators calculated but do not see why shared variable factors appear only once in the lowest common denominator. Multiplying the denominators would also work, concealing this distinction.
findings.checked: Earlier teaching supplies equivalent fractions with a given target denominator and cancellation. p8 names the lowest common multiple, but its examples and first two guided parts supply it without explaining its algebraic construction.
findings.assumptions: Numerical lowest common multiples are prior knowledge; choosing them for algebraic terms is new in the supplied teaching.

repair.proposal: Before the examples' supplied denominators, add: “For the lowest common denominator, use the numerical LCM and the highest power of each variable present. For 5 and a², this gives 5a².” Then: “For 3x and 5x, LCM(3, 5) = 15 and the highest power of x is x, so use 15x.”

findings.doneWhen: The examples connect their original denominators to the chosen common denominators and explain the treatment of shared variable factors.

findings.finding: Extend the rectangle task by doubling both dimensions and comparing areas.
findings.breakdown: The existing context supports a concrete comparison between doubling each factor and multiplying the area by four.
findings.checked: The original dimensions are 3x/5 and 12x/5 cm, giving area 36x²/25 cm². The doubled dimensions give area 144x²/25 cm². Only taught multiplication and simplification are needed.
findings.assumptions: The rectangle context requires x > 0, so its original area is nonzero and the area ratio is defined.

repair.proposal: After the existing area task, append: (b) A second rectangle has twice the width and twice the length of the first. Write its width and length. Answers: 6x/5 cm and 24x/5 cm. (c) Find its area. Answer: 144x²/25 cm². (d) How many times the original area is this? Answer: 4 times.

findings.doneWhen: The optional follow-up uses the original rectangle and compares the two areas.

protectedGroups.observation: Factor order does not affect a product, and common factors can cancel across either fraction while unmatched factors remain.
protectedGroups.varies: Factor order, one coefficient or the location and multiplicity of a denominator factor.
protectedGroups.invariant: Multiplication of two fractions using the same core pronumerals.

protectedGroups.observation: Dividing by a fraction has the same effect as multiplying by its reciprocal.
protectedGroups.varies: The operation and the orientation of the second fraction.
protectedGroups.invariant: The first fraction and the factors appearing in the second fraction.

protectedGroups.observation: Operation signs and grouping determine which fractions are reciprocated; similar-looking expressions can therefore have different values.
protectedGroups.varies: One operation, exponent, grouping or coefficient at a time, followed by an exchange of operations.
protectedGroups.invariant: The three-fraction structure and most of its factors.

protectedGroups.observation: Multiplying by 1/x and dividing by 1/x have different effects.
Corresponding addition and subtraction tasks preserve the denominator decisions while changing the operation.
protectedGroups.varies: Addition versus subtraction in each corresponding pair.
protectedGroups.invariant: The fractions and their common denominator within each pair.

protectedGroups.observation: The sequence isolates a numerator change, then the operation, then subtraction order.
protectedGroups.varies: One numerator coefficient, addition versus subtraction, then fraction order.
protectedGroups.invariant: The denominator pair 2 and 5 and the common pronumeral numerator factor.

protectedGroups.observation: Changing x² to xy exposes which missing pronumeral factor is needed; the next part changes only a numerical denominator coefficient.
protectedGroups.varies: One pronumeral factor, then one numerical coefficient.
protectedGroups.invariant: Numerators 6 and 2, addition, and the first denominator's coefficient 2.

protectedGroups.observation: Cancelling identical variable factors can leave 1, a whole-number coefficient or a numerical fraction.
protectedGroups.invariant: Both numerator and denominator contain a single factor x.

protectedGroups.observation: A variable appearing on only one side of the fraction bar remains on that side after numerical reduction.
protectedGroups.varies: The presence and position of x.

protectedGroups.observation: A matching denominator variable cancels, changing a numerical coefficient changes only its quotient, and an unmatched numerator variable remains.
protectedGroups.varies: One denominator factor, then the denominator coefficient, then an additional numerator variable.
protectedGroups.invariant: The numerator retains the factor 12x and each adjacent pair changes one feature.

protectedGroups.observation: Matching powers cancel factor by factor, so a variable can remain below the bar, disappear or remain above it as its numerator exponent increases.
protectedGroups.varies: One variable exponent at each step.
protectedGroups.invariant: The numerical coefficients remain 10 and 12, and the denominator retains x throughout.

importReview: Lean content review table: 45 of 45 blocks passed.

dropped.reason: The central-relationship test defeats this suggestion. Its mathematics is correct for x > 0, but the relationship exposed is area scaling when both dimensions double, rather than a relationship central to multiplying and dividing algebraic fractions.

candidates.finding: Use the same rectangle to compare doubling its width with the resulting change in area.
